analysis.one_liner: Extends overtime, sick pay, breaks, written contracts, and civil rights protections to domestic workers.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate committee it was sent to, and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would give an estimated 2.2 million domestic workers — nannies, housekeepers, home health aides, and caregivers — basic workplace rights most other workers already have. It would repeal the federal exemption that denies live-in domestic workers overtime pay, require written work agreements, guarantee up to 56 hours of earned paid sick time a year, mandate meal and rest breaks, protect workers from retaliation and immigration threats, extend Title VII anti-discrimination law to them, and raise the federal Medicaid matching rate to help cover the cost in publicly funded home care. It also bans forced arbitration and nondisclosure clauses in these workers' contracts.
analysis.who_benefits: Domestic workers — about 9 in 10 of whom are women, disproportionately women of color and immigrants, earning an average of roughly $13.79 an hour, often with no contract, sick leave, or overtime. Older people and people with disabilities who receive Medicaid-funded home care would also benefit from the bill's higher federal Medicaid match and protections tied to publicly funded care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Domestic workers, mostly women of color

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Fair Labor Standards Act section that has excluded live-in domestic workers from overtime pay, and requires termination notice plus 30 days of lodging or two weeks' severance for fired live-in workers.

Requires a signed, plain-language written agreement for any domestic worker employed 8 or more hours a week, covering pay, hours, breaks, termination policy, and privacy rules, and bans predispute arbitration and nondisclosure or noncompete clauses in those agreements.

Grants at least 1 hour of paid sick time per 30 hours worked, capped at 56 hours a year, usable for the worker's own illness, care for family, or situations involving domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Requires 72 hours' notice of schedule changes with partial pay for canceled hours, guarantees meal breaks after 5 hours and paid rest breaks every 4 hours, and bars wage deductions for cash shortages or broken household items.

Extends Title VII of the Civil Rights Act to domestic employees who are currently excluded in practice, and makes it unlawful to retaliate against workers — including by threatening to report their immigration status — for asserting these rights.

Creates a Domestic Employee Standards Board, a national hotline, an enforcement task force, and community outreach grants, and temporarily raises the federal Medicaid matching rate for publicly funded home care provided by domestic workers.

analysis.who_pays: Households that employ nannies, housekeepers, and aides would owe overtime, sick pay, and compliance paperwork, and families paying out of pocket for in-home care would likely face higher prices. Medicaid's increased federal match would be a cost to federal taxpayers, and home care agencies would absorb new wage and scheduling obligations.
analysis.who_pays_short: Employing households, care agencies, and Medicaid

drawbacks.text: The paid sick time, schedule-change pay, and overtime mandates would raise the cost of in-home child care and elder care, which middle- and lower-income families pay for largely out of pocket; the bill provides no offset for private households, only for Medicaid-funded care.

The rules apply to individual households, not just agencies, so ordinary families hiring a babysitter-level employee for 8 or more hours a week would need written multi-page agreements and could face $5,000 liability for paperwork violations.

The bill gives the Labor Secretary broad rulemaking authority over a workforce spread across millions of private homes, and critics of comparable state laws have argued enforcement in private residences raises privacy and practicality concerns.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly 2.2 million workers covered — earning near $14 an hour with less than 9 percent having payroll taxes paid toward Social Security — the bill addresses real, documented gaps: 91 percent of workers in one landmark study who faced problems said they stayed silent for fear of losing their job. The costs fall on the households and agencies that hire them, and since care is a necessity, higher in-home care costs would land partly back on working families who buy it. The bill tries to soften this with Medicaid funding, disaster and emergency exceptions, and carve-outs for shared living arrangements, but it does not subsidize private families' higher costs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never held a hearing or vote on it before the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Gillibrand introduced the Domestic Workers Bill of Rights Act on June 13, 2024, with 16 Senate Democrats and one Independent joining as original cosponsors.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on the day of introduction; that was the last action of any kind in its action history.
No markup, hearing, committee vote, or floor vote appears in the record, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, ending the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Households and home care agencies that employ domestic workers keep the current cost structure, with no new overtime, sick pay, or contract obligations; the workers whose conditions the bill documented remain covered only by the state laws that exist today.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Households and agencies that employ domestic workers

for.name: Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: U.S. Senator from New York; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered 17 cosponsors, all Democrats or Independents, on the day of introduction.

for.name: 16 of 48 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including Senators Baldwin, Blumenthal, Casey, Duckworth, Durbin, Fetterman, Kaine, Klobuchar, Markey, Merkley, and Warren.

for.name: Bernie Sanders
for.role: U.S. Senator from Vermont; chaired the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill but his committee did not hold a markup or vote on it during the remainder of the Congress.

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of referral for labor bills
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — leaving the bill to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 17 cosponsors were Senate Democrats or Independents; no Senate Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past committee referral.

industries.note: Agencies employing aides and housekeepers would owe overtime, sick time, scheduling notice pay, and written contracts, raising their labor costs; the Medicaid match increase would partially offset costs on the publicly funded side. Their interest in avoiding these mandates runs against the workers' interest in them.

The bill bars employers from penalizing workers who communicate directly with customers instead of through the platform's app or messaging system, and pulls platform-arranged domestic work into the written-agreement and pay-protection rules.

Families hiring nannies, housekeepers, or aides for 8 or more hours a week would face contract requirements, overtime and sick pay obligations, and up to $5,000 liability for missing paperwork, raising the price of in-home care they pay out of pocket.

The bill applies its worker protections to Medicaid-funded services and temporarily raises the federal Medicaid matching rate to pay for them, routing federal money through home care providers to fund better conditions for the workers delivering that care.
